coherence.reasons: Both run the same logical spine: market grows but loses money, unit economics are negative on observed inputs, the plan needs unobserved inputs, runway is broken, so choose software. X's summary maps one-to-one onto its slides, and slide 3 tests the founders' three claims explicitly before the evidence pages. Its density message is consistent throughout: density explains only a fifth of the gap, and about 6,400 orders a day would be needed. Y is also well ordered, with sub-questions leading to sections and an answer, but it has small internal slips. Slide 10 claims a loss 'even before the dark store is paid for' and evidences it with the after-site-cost figure. Slide 26 says 'density, not store count, is the lever', while slide 34 says no amount of density fixes the loss per order. Y's governing thought also rests on a software break-even projection that sits on backup assumptions.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the same defensible recommendation: decline the launch, fund the software business, and set reopen triggers. Both reject the nine-store plan and a one-store pilot for sound reasons, and neither is drawn into a 'prove density' launch. Y goes further in showing the alternative meets the investors' test: it models software break-even in early 2029 with about $5.4M left and runway of about two years, and it tests the one-store pilot on top of the software plan (10.2 months). Its four gates have owners and include core-business break-even, and it plans a pilot of store-based delivery with a grocer. X asserts that software 'meets both conditions' without modelling a path to profit. X is more candid that flat burn reaches the floor in about 18 months and that burn must fall whatever the board decides, and its promotions cap on the reopen trigger is a sensible detail. Y's weighing of the alternative is slightly more complete, though it leans on optimistic assumptions.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical figures right: −$6.17 at median, −$1.76 for the best composite, about −$12.57 for the pop-up, +$2.02 for the plan, $2.5M or about 6 months of runway, and −$1.05 for the Zipcart playbook. Every figure I recomputed in both documents checked out. X adds more decision-relevant tests: best of everything with 2% promotions (−$0.08), density needed at the best margin (about 6,400 a day), the pop-up at 900 a day (−$9.71), the strict cash reading (−$4.7M), payback across four cases, and nine-store results across cases. It also states the 41.5% compound growth rate and makes the sharp inference that the 14 benchmark sites already run Parcelbird software, so any software edge is already in the numbers. Y adds a break-even basket ($63), a basket-by-productivity grid, 20% sensitivities and a rider-pay sensitivity. However, Y puts a three-year projection (60% growth sustained, costs flat) into its governing thought, which is a weakly supported claim even though it is flagged in backup, and it gives only year-on-year growth, not the compound rate. X's title 'nothing in the evidence supports +$2' slightly overreaches, because a Zipcart-style fee at the best observed density would exceed that; neither document tests that case. X is more careful overall about what it claims.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the evidence while accepting the growth claim. X handles it more directly: slide 3 gives a verdict on each of the three claims (growth holds; 'we run them better' not supported; 'density makes it positive' not supported). It rebuts the operating-edge claim with two points: the benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software, and the pop-up underperformed them. It also shows density explains only about a fifth of the gap. Y engages more fully with the supporting Zipcart evidence, giving it a dedicated case slide and concluding that 'pricing can close most of the gap' but lost orders keep it negative. Y also flags that 'nobody owns the Midwest' is untested. But Y never directly tests the 'we know how to run them better' claim. Neither computes the fee case at best observed density. X's claim-by-claim treatment is the more appropriate handling overall.

overall.reasons: The two documents are close: same defensible recommendation, same core calculations done correctly, same rejected alternatives, and similar reopen gates. X is tighter and more rigorous per claim. It tests the founders' claims one by one, adds several stress tests showing that even generous combinations fail, and is candid about the core business's own runway problem. Y's distinctive strengths are the modelled software path to break-even, which speaks directly to the investors' objective, and gates with named owners. That path rests on optimistic assumptions that Y promotes to its headline, and the document has minor internal inconsistencies on density. On reasoning quality, X serves the board slightly better.
